stem: During an audit of a standalone AWS account, a small design agency learns that the root user has an active access key used by a nightly backup script and has no MFA device. Which action best addresses both findings?

choices.text: Move the script to an IAM role, delete the root access key, and register MFA for the root user
Keep the root access key, rotate it every 90 days, and store it in AWS Secrets Manager
Register MFA for the root user and keep the access key, because scripts cannot use MFA anyway
Move the script to an IAM role, delete the root access key, and set the account password policy to require MFA

rationale: AWS recommends that you do not create access keys for the root user, that you protect root sign-in with MFA, and that you use the root user only for tasks that require it. Workloads should use the temporary credentials of an IAM role, so moving the script to a role lets you delete the key. Rotating and storing the root key still leaves a long-term credential with full access to every service and billing. Adding MFA protects console sign-in, but the access key would keep working without MFA, so the most dangerous credential remains. Moving the script to a role and deleting the root access key correctly fixes the access-key finding, but setting the account password policy to require MFA does not fix the other finding: the IAM password policy controls password length, complexity, expiration, and reuse, has no MFA setting, and does not apply to the root user, so the root user still has no MFA device registered.
